data.title: Justice and Terror in Rome
sentences: Roman law maintained order through public displays of brutal retribution.
Crucifixion, known as the extreme punishment, was reserved for slaves and rebels to instill absolute terror.
Victims were scourged before being nailed to a cross, suffering until death by asphyxiation.
Constantine the Great finally abolished this practice in the fourth century.
For the crime of parricide, Romans enacted the punishment of the sack.
Offenders were sewn into a leather bag with a dog, a rooster, a viper, and a monkey before being cast into water.
This ritual symbolized the murderer's bestial nature.
Finally, the arena hosted the horror of condemnation to the beasts.
Commoners and Christians were thrown to lions and bears for public entertainment.
These punishments reinforced the state's power, while the elite enjoyed the privilege of a dignified beheading.
For the rest of the Roman populace, the law offered only a slow, gruesome end.
